passages.original: 5. Pyrrhichium dictum esse alii dicunt a Pyrrho, Achillis filio, quem primum aiunt in tumulo patris sui armatum honoris gratia saltavisse. 502 Aristoteles autem Achillem ait hujus ludi inventorem inisse. Quibusdam placet ab ardore, id est, ab ipsa velocitate sui soni nomen accepisse hunc pedem, ἀπὸ του πυρὸς, id est, ab hac flammæ velocitate. Cognatio enim ardoris et velocitatis est;
passages.english: 5. Some say that the pyrrhic was named after Pyrrhus, the son of Achilles, who they say was the first to dance in arms at his father's tomb, for the sake of honour. Aristotle, however, says that Achilles was the inventor of this game. Some hold that this foot took its name from ardour, that is, from the very swiftness of its sound, apo tou pyros [from fire], that is, from this swiftness of flame. For ardour and swiftness are related;
passages.notes: "502" is a page number from the printed edition and is omitted. "inisse" is probably an error for "fuisse" ("was"); it is translated so.

passages.original: Ipsa tamen a pyrrhiacha dicta , id est, lusione, vel Pyrrhichia filia, vel a Pyrrhicho, qui primus CretenseM sub armis saltare in hujus pedis sonum constituit. Spondeus tamen nomen ac;cepit a sacrificio, quia spondeon Græce sacrificium nuncupatur, quo sono hymnos, id est, laudes diis immortalibus decantabant; unde et Homerus ait : Sponde tua Crete.
passages.english: It [the pyrrhic dance], however, is named from *pyrrhiacha*, that is, play, or from Pyrrhichia the daughter, or from Pyrrhichus, who first established that the Cretans should dance in arms to the sound of this foot. The spondee, however, took its name from sacrifice, because in Greek a sacrifice is called *spondeon*, and to this sound they used to chant hymns, that is, praises, to the immortal gods; hence Homer also says: "Sponde tua Crete."
passages.notes: *pyrrhiacha* is an obscure form and may be corrupt. The Homeric citation "Sponde tua Crete" is garbled and its meaning is unclear, so it is left untranslated. "CretenseM" is a scanning error for "Cretenses" (the Cretans).

passages.original: Undecimo anno ibat edictio in Asiam, et per quinque annorum spatia exigebatur census Caesari, et completis quinque annis, iterum quindecimo anno effundebatur census in area custodiae Capitolii, et dicebatur ille annus indictio, quia per ter quinque annos ex tribus partibus mundi census exigebatur. Ub hanc causam super quindecim annis indictio non graditur, et completis quindecim annis, alia indictio incipit, de quo Macrobius dicit : Indictio dicta eat reipublicæ exactio ; id est, census totius orbis terrarum in urbe Roma complebatur, et tunc septenis diebus, completis quindecim annis, urbs Roma illustrabatur.
passages.english: In the eleventh year the edict went out into Asia, and over a span of five years the tax was exacted for Caesar; and when the five years were completed, again in the fifteenth year the tax was poured out in the treasury area of the Capitol, and that year was called the indiction, because over three times five years the tax was exacted from the three parts of the world. For this reason the indiction does not proceed beyond fifteen years, and when fifteen years are completed, another indiction begins. About this Macrobius says: "The indiction is so called [as being] the exaction of the state"; that is, the tax of the whole world was completed in the city of Rome, and then, when the fifteen years were completed, the city of Rome was purified for seven days at a time.
passages.notes: "Ub hanc causam" read as "Ob hanc causam"; "dicta eat" read as "dicta est" (scanning errors). "In area custodiae Capitolii" is uncertain: possibly "in the strongroom (or courtyard) of the Capitol". "Illustrabatur" is taken in the sense of lustration (ritual purification); it could also mean "was illuminated" or "made splendid". The attribution to Macrobius is as the text gives it; the quoted wording is not verified.

passages.original: I. Sed sicut Dumioi Natale quocunque die venerit, VIII Kal. Januarii, ita et VIII KaJ. Aprilis, quando resurrectio traditur Christi, debemus Pascha tenere. Orientales vero, sicut historia Eusebii Cæsariensis narrat, quocunque die mensis Martii xiv luna venis set, Pascba celebrabant.
passages.english: I. But just as [we keep] the Lord's Nativity on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, on whatever day of the week it falls, so also we ought to keep Easter on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, when the resurrection of Christ is handed down [as having happened]. The Easterners, however, as the history of Eusebius of Caesarea relates, used to celebrate Easter on whatever day of the month of March the fourteenth moon fell.
passages.notes: "Dumioi" is read as "Domini" (the Lord's). The eighth day before the Kalends of January is 25 December; the eighth day before the Kalends of April is 25 March.

passages.original: 2. Duodecima species definitionis e-t quam Græci ϰατ' ἐπαινὸν vocant, id est, per laudem, ut Tullius pro Cluentio : Lex est mens, et consilium, et animus, et sen entia civitatis. Et alter : Pax est tranquilla libertas. Fit et per vituperationem, quam græci ψόγον vocant, ut servitus est postremum omnium malorum, non modo bello, sed morte quoque.
passages.english: 2. The twelfth kind of definition is the one the Greeks call *kat' epainon*, that is, by praise, as Tully [Cicero] in his speech for Cluentius: "Law is the mind, and the counsel, and the spirit, and the judgement of the state." And another: "Peace is tranquil liberty." It is also made by censure, which the Greeks call *psogos*, as: "Slavery is the last of all evils, [to be repelled] not only by war but even by death."
passages.notes: The final sentence is completed by "repellenda", which falls in the following context. "e-t" and "sen entia" are scanning errors for "est" and "sententia".

passages.original: Secundum musicam ita : quot partes superat medium primum, eadem parte 543 superatur medium ab extremo, ut puta, vi et VIII duabus partibus superant, quae duæ partes tertia media octus (SIC) superatur ab ultima nona figuras solidas. Planae figuræ sunt, quæ longitudine et latitudine continentur. Quæ sunt juxta Platonem numero quinque. Numerabilis magnitudo est quae numeris arithmeticæ dividi potest. Magnitudines rationales sunt quorum mensuræ quantitas cognita nOli habetur.
passages.english: According to music, thus: by as many parts as the middle exceeds the first, by the same part the middle is exceeded by the extreme. For example, 6 and 8 exceed by two parts, which two parts [...] the middle eight is exceeded by the last, nine [...] solid figures. Plane figures are those contained by length and breadth, and according to Plato they are five in number. A numerable magnitude is one that can be divided by the numbers of arithmetic. Rational magnitudes are those whose quantity of measure is held as known.
passages.notes: The middle sentence is corrupt (the edition itself marks it "SIC") and is translated only in fragments. Some corrupt words, including "tertia" and "figuras solidas", are left without connection. "nOli" in the last sentence is unclear and is omitted. "543" is a page number from the printed edition and is omitted.

passages.original: 26. Beatissimus Hieronymus in commentariis Zachariae ita sic dicit : Festi autem dies in veteri lege isti sunt : Dies Azymorum phase quarta : decima die mensis primi est, quando luna plenissima ab ejecto fermento agnus immolatur.
passages.english: 26. The most blessed Jerome, in his commentaries on Zechariah, speaks thus: "Now these are the feast days in the old law: the day of Unleavened Bread, the Passover, [...] on the fourteenth day of the first month, when, at the fullest moon, after the leaven has been cast out, the lamb is sacrificed."
passages.notes: "phase quarta : decima" is read as "Phase, quarta decima" (Passover, the fourteenth). The construction of the quotation is somewhat garbled, and "ita sic" is redundant.
